title: Availability vs representativeness heuristic

a.definition: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

b.definition: Judging whether A belongs to class B by how much A resembles B.

diff: Ask what supplies the shortcut. Remembered examples mean availability, and similarity to a type means representativeness. Heuristics are rapid rules of thumb that are likely to give a correct answer but are not foolproof.
example: A botulism death in the news makes it seem likelier than asthma (availability). Robert resembling a librarian makes people say librarian (representativeness).
watch: Memorability is also affected by distinctiveness and emotion, which do not make an event more common.

title: Base rate vs description information

a.definition: The background prevalence of categories, such as 70 lawyers and 30 engineers, or about 2.2 million farms and 120,000 libraries.

b.definition: Personal characteristics that resemble a category, such as Jack's hobbies or Robert's glasses and quiet speech.

diff: People use the base rate correctly when it is all they have, but disregard it once a description is given. That is base-rate neglect, where similarity displaces the prevalence of the categories.
example: With only the 70/30 split people say 30 in 100. After Jack is described as careful and enjoying mathematical puzzles, they call him an engineer.
watch: The base rate favors farmer for Robert even though he fits the librarian description.

title: Conjunction rule vs representativeness

a.definition: Two things together can never be more probable than either alone, because every case where both are true is also a case where each is true.

b.definition: Judging by how well a description fits a typical case, so a more detailed story that fits the person better feels more probable.

diff: One is a rule about nested sets and the other is a shortcut by resemblance. They conflict when the combined description fits better than its single part. About 82 percent chose that Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement over bank teller alone, but feminist bank tellers are a subset of bank tellers.
example: Linda is single, outspoken, bright, trained in philosophy and active in antinuclear demonstrations.
watch: More detail can make a story fit better but never makes it more probable.

title: Number of winners vs probability of winning

a.term: Attending to the number of favorable items
a.definition: Seven red beans looks like more chances than one red bean.

b.definition: Seven in 100 is 7 percent and one in 10 is 10 percent, so the bowl with fewer red beans is better.

diff: A larger number of favorable items draws attention away from the denominator, the total number of possible draws. The decision then depends on considerations other than the actual probabilities of winning.
example: In the jellybean problem a participant earns one dollar for each red bean drawn, and most participants chose the 7-out-of-100 bowl over the 1-out-of-10 bowl.

title: Small sample vs large sample

a.definition: About 45 births a day, so its daily proportion of boys is more stable.

b.definition: About 15 births a day, so extreme proportions are more likely.

diff: The correct answer is the smaller hospital for more days with over 60 percent boys. The most common response, chosen by 56 percent, was about the same. The law of large numbers says larger random samples become more representative, and people wrongly expect small samples to be representative too.
example: Half of all babies are boys, but a single day's 15 births swing more than 45 births.
watch: Do not confuse the absolute number of boys with how often an extreme proportion occurs.

title: Confirmation bias vs myside bias

a.definition: Seeking information that fits a hypothesis and overlooking what argues against it.

b.definition: Generating and evaluating evidence, and testing hypotheses, in ways biased toward one's own opinions and attitudes.

diff: Myside bias is one form of confirmation bias, tied to one's own opinions. In Lord and colleagues (1979), people for and against capital punishment read the same article and each side interpreted it as favoring their own position.
example: The 2, 4, 6 task shows confirmation bias. The capital punishment article shows myside bias.
watch: Myside bias is a form of confirmation bias, not a different bias.

title: Testing what fits vs trying to disconfirm (2, 4, 6)

a.definition: Writing sets that fit the hypothesis, such as increasing by two, which keeps returning yes.

b.definition: Testing the boundaries of the belief to find where it breaks.

diff: The most common hypothesis is increasing intervals of two, but the actual rule is any three numbers in increasing order. Only trying to disconfirm reveals that the narrow belief is wrong.
example: Participants write their own sets and get feedback only on whether each fits.
watch: Repeated yes feedback does not confirm a rule that is too narrow.

title: Taboo tradeoff vs tragic tradeoff

a.definition: Mixes sacred and secular domains, such as a child's life against money. It provokes moral outrage.

b.definition: Compares two sacred values with each other. People are less morally outraged.

diff: The Sacred Value Protection Model (Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green and Lerner, 2000) says sacred values are compartmentalized from secular ones. Ask whether the competing item is a secular benefit (taboo) or another sacred value (tragic).
example: Johnny's liver costing one million dollars (taboo) versus two children and one available liver (tragic).
watch: A tragic tradeoff still involves a hard choice, but it does not threaten the sacred-secular boundary.

title: Outrage by tradeoff type and decision (Tetlock and colleagues, 2000)

a.definition: A sacred value (Johnny's life) is weighed against a secular benefit (one million dollars). Not saving Johnny drew much greater outrage than saving him, and spending the money on other uses instead of the child received the strongest negative response.

b.definition: Two sacred values compete (two children, one available liver). Outrage was similar whether Johnny was saved or not, because either choice leaves a sacred concern unmet.

diff: How outraged people are depends on both the type of value conflict and the decision made within it, and that interaction is the finding.
example: Tetlock and colleagues (2000) rated moral outrage for each combination of tradeoff type and decision.
watch: Do not say outrage depends only on the decision. It depends on the type of conflict as well.

title: Moral absolutists vs non-absolutists

a.definition: Treat the issue as a sacred value and reject compromise regardless of benefit.

b.definition: Have strong preferences against compromise but do not treat the issue as sacred.

diff: Ask whether benefits can enter the decision at all, not how much the person cares. For absolutists, adding money increased anger, disgust and support for violence, while for non-absolutists it reduced them.
example: Ginges, Atran, Medin and Shikaki (2007) studied 601 Israeli settlers, 535 Palestinian refugees and 719 Palestinian students.
watch: Absolutists are not just people who feel strongly. Their issue is sacred.

title: Money vs symbolic recognition

a.definition: Money added to the deal, such as one billion dollars a year for ten years.

b.definition: Israeli recognition of the historic and legitimate right of Palestinians to their own state and an apology for wrongs done.

diff: Money changes the economic benefit, and symbolic terms address the status of a group's claim. In Ginges, Atran, Medin and Shikaki (2007), money raised absolutists' anger, and the symbolic offer was associated with lower anger and lower support for violence.
example: Ginges, Atran, Medin and Shikaki (2007) added to the deal either one billion dollars a year for ten years or the recognition and apology.
watch: Material benefit and symbolic reciprocity are different.

title: Incentive (Taboo+) vs disincentive (Taboo−)

a.definition: A benefit offered for agreeing, such as 40 billion dollars from the United Nations.

b.definition: A cost imposed for refusing, such as the threat of additional sanctions.

diff: Incentives change the benefit of accepting, and disincentives change the cost of refusing. In the study by Dehghani and colleagues (2009, 2010), participants with a sacred value showed lower approval for energy with both the incentive and the sanction than with the baseline.
example: Dehghani and colleagues (2009, 2010) asked Iranian participants about a deal to give up their nuclear program, with or without an incentive or a sanction.
watch: For a sacred commitment, improving the material balance does not improve acceptability.

title: Participants with vs without a sacred value (Dehghani)

a.definition: Said giving up the program should not be done no matter the consequences. About 14 percent for energy and 13 percent for weapons.

b.definition: Had much higher approval and lower anger, with little variation across conditions.

diff: For energy, anticipated anger was highest with the incentive and elevated with sanctions for those holding a sacred value. For participants without a sacred value, the deals barely mattered.
example: Dehghani, Atran and colleagues (2010) and Dehghani, Iliev and colleagues (2009) used a measure based on Baron and Spranca (1997).
watch: Only a small share of participants held the value as sacred, but they responded differently.

title: Net lives saved vs reluctance to cause a loss

a.definition: Choosing the option that saves more overall. Rerouting the convoy saves 1,000 at a second camp and costs 100 at the first, a net of 900.

b.definition: Resisting an action that makes others die even when more are saved elsewhere. In Ritov and Baron (1999), 63 percent did not choose to reroute.

diff: Counting treats the lives lost by acting and the lives lost by not acting the same, but many people do not, and some would keep the original route even if only one person at the first camp would die. The better net count did not decide the choice.
example: In the convoy dilemma, food trucks are traveling to a refugee camp during a famine.
watch: The better net count did not decide the choice.

title: Expected utility theory vs real choices

a.definition: Assumes rational people with all relevant information choose the option with the highest expected utility, which combines how valuable each outcome is with its chance. The monetary version uses the highest expected payoff.

b.definition: People find value in things other than money, and many decisions do not maximize the probability of the best outcome.

diff: The theory gives a procedure for the best choice, but people are not utility-maximization machines, so it describes what a maximizer would do and not what people do.
example: Casino gambling: people choose it despite knowing the odds are strongly against them.
watch: Utility is how desirable an outcome is to the person, which is not the same as money.

title: Easy to recall vs actually frequent (availability)

a.definition: Events or words that are distinctive, emotionally salient or retrieved easily, which makes them feel more numerous.

b.definition: How often the event or word really occurs.

diff: About 70 percent say English has more words beginning with r than words with r as the third letter, but r-third words are about three times more common. A death from botulism can be front-page news while asthma deaths go virtually unnoticed, so people pick the less likely cause.
example: Retrieving words by first letter is easier, so those words feel more numerous.

title: Illusory correlation vs a real association

a.definition: A relationship that appears to exist even though it does not exist or is much weaker than assumed.

b.definition: A relationship that is actually present in the data.

diff: Stereotypes direct attention to behaviors that fit the expected description, and remembering the matching instances makes the stereotype feel supported. Stereotype-consistent behaviors are easier to bring to mind, and their availability is mistaken for evidence that the behavior is strongly associated with the group.
example: A stereotype feels confirmed because the fitting instances were noticed and retained.
watch: The apparent evidence is shaped by what was noticed and remembered.

title: Feared event vs actual risk (after September 11)

a.definition: The fear produced by the attacks led to a decision based on how the event felt.

b.definition: The probability of dying in a car accident is much greater than while flying.

diff: After September 11, air travel decreased and driving increased. The reported number of Americans who died on the road while avoiding flying exceeded the total number of passengers killed on the four hijacked flights.
example: Avoiding the feared event increased exposure to a more likely danger.
watch: Emotional impact and probability are different bases for a decision.

title: Decision vs judgment vs reasoning

a.definition: The process of choosing between alternatives.

b.definition: Reasoning is the process of drawing conclusions, and decisions are based on the judgments people make.

diff: Inductive reasoning, from observations to conclusions that are probably but not definitely true, is one of the primary mechanisms involved in making judgments.
example: In everyday life people use past experience to predict what will happen, especially in familiar situations.
watch: A decision is a choice, and a judgment is an estimate that feeds it.
